section.md: \text{what accumulates inside an interval is measured by what happens on its boundary.}
section.p: In one dimension, the boundary of an interval consists of two endpoints. The right endpoint counts positively. The left endpoint counts negatively.
That signed boundary is the seed of Stokes’ theorem.

exercise.title: Why is the boundary of an interval two signed endpoints?

statement.p: The oriented interval from a to b has boundary \{b\}-\{a\}. In your own words, why does direction matter, and why do those opposite signs make split intervals add correctly?

hint.p: Traveling from a to b arrives at b and leaves a. If you split at an interior point, the extra interior endpoint is counted plus and then minus, so it cancels.

paragraphs.title: Warning: jumps are not ordinary derivatives
paragraphs.p: The theorem requires F to be differentiable on the interval. If F jumps, the ordinary derivative does not capture the jump.
But H is not differentiable at 0. Away from 0, it is constant, so its derivative is 0 where the derivative exists.
If we tried to integrate the ordinary derivative away from the jump, we would get
The missing change is concentrated at the jump. Ordinary single-variable calculus does not represent that jump as an ordinary derivative. This is why the differentiability hypothesis matters.
paragraphs.md: \text{The Fundamental Theorem applies to honest derivatives, not to hidden jumps.}

exercise.title: Why is the Fundamental Theorem a boundary theorem?

statement.p: The identity \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a) says that what accumulates inside is measured by the signed boundary. In your own words, why is that a geometric reading rather than only an antiderivative rule, and why do hidden jumps refuse to be ordinary derivatives?

hint.p: The interior contributions telescope, leaving only the ending value minus the starting value. A jump is not produced by a continuous derivative, so the theorem’s hypotheses are part of the geometry.

paragraphs.title: Exact integrands
paragraphs.p: When an integrand is exact, its integral depends only on the boundary:
This is exactly what an antiderivative does. Finding an antiderivative is finding a function F whose differential is the integrand.

exercise.title: What does it mean for an integrand to be exact?

statement.p: An integrand of the form dF=F'(x)\,dx is exact, and its integral depends only on the boundary. In your own words, why is finding an antiderivative the same as recognizing an exact differential, and why does that make interior cancellations the whole story?

hint.p: If every small piece is a change in F, adding the pieces is telescoping. Only the two ends survive, which is exactly what an antiderivative computes.

In higher dimensions, this becomes a real question: not every integrand is exact. That is one reason the boundary viewpoint becomes powerful.
